title: Selector Strategy and Best Practices knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Selector Strategy and Best Practices”?
options: Selector specificity at a basic level
questions.answer_key: Selector specificity at a basic level
questions.explanation: The source curriculum lists “Selector specificity at a basic level” under “Selector Strategy and Best Practices”. The lesson applies this syllabus point to a small CSS example and a browser check.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports reliable work with selector strategy and best practices?
options: Use the simplest selector that clearly identifies the intended elements, then check the match set.
Add !important to every declaration so conflicts disappear.
Assume the newest CSS feature behaves identically in all browsers.
Remove focus styles because a mouse user can see the hovered element.
questions.answer_key: Use the simplest selector that clearly identifies the intended elements, then check the match set.
questions.explanation: The key practice is: Use the simplest selector that clearly identifies the intended elements, then check the match set. For advanced features, inspect the relevant documentation and target-browser compatibility.

questions.prompt: If an example related to “Selector Strategy and Best Practices” does not look or behave as expected, what is the strongest first response?
options: Inspect the matched and computed styles, change one cause, and retest the original scenario.
Add several unrelated overrides until the screenshot looks closer.
Only check the default viewport and skip interactive states.
Treat an unused declaration as proof that the browser is broken.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the matched and computed styles, change one cause, and retest the original scenario.
questions.explanation: A repeatable inspection loop is more reliable than layering on overrides: inspect what matched, identify the computed value, change one cause, and retest.
